The polarization of macrophages, key immune cells, is influenced by implant surface characteristics. This research aimed to examine periodontal ligament mesenchymal stromal cells (PDL MSCs) responses to the polarized macrophages induced by titanium surface roughness. Materials and Methods RAW 264.7 macrophages were cultured with various surface roughness of titanium disks. Macrophage adhesion and polarization were evaluated by scanning electron microscope, gene expressions profiling, and flow cytometry. PDL MSCs were treated with conditioned medium of macrophages and analyzed with 3-[4,5-dimethylthiazol-2yl]-2,5-diphenyl-2H-tetrazolium bromide assay, real-time polymerase chain reaction, and Alizarin red staining. Statistical Analysis Data was statistically analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9 for Windows 11. The one-way analysis of variance test was used to compare the groups. Dunn post hoc test was used to compare the difference between the groups when appropriate. Significance was accepted when p < 0.05. fetched_contents.text: Animal Models for Investigating Osseointegration: An Overview of Implant Research over the Last Three Decades Abstract Dental implants and bone augmentation are among dentistry’s most prevalent surgical treatments; hence, many dental implant surfaces and bone grafts have been researched to improve bone response. Such new materials were radiologically, histologically, and histomorphometrically evaluated on animals before being used on humans. As a result, several studies used animals to evaluate novel implant technologies, biocompatibility, surgical techniques, and osseointegration strategies, as preclinical research on animal models is essential to evaluate bioactive principles (on cells, compounds, and implants) that can act through multiple mechanisms and to predict animal behavior, which is difficult to predict from in vitro studies alone. In this study, we critically reviewed all research on different animal models investigating the osseointegration degree of new implant surfaces, reporting different species used in the osseointegration research over the last 30 years. Moreover, this is the first study to summarize reviews on the main animal models used in the translational research of osseointegration, including the advantages and limitations of each model and determining the ideal location for investigating osseointegration in small and large animal models. Overall, each model has advantages and disadvantages; hence, animal selection should be based on the cost of acquisition, animal care, acceptability to society, availability, tolerance to captivity, and housing convenience. Among small animal models, rabbits are an ideal model for biological observations around implants, and it is worth noting that osseointegration was discovered in the rabbit model and successfully applied to humans. Keywords: ARRIVE guidelines, biomaterial, dental implants, in vivo studies, osseointegration, preclinical studies, regenerative medicine, translational research 1. Introduction Literature has revealed a high success rate (90–95%) of dental implants after five years of loading (including bone regeneration), and they are often used to rehabilitate partial or complete edentulous patients since dental implants are an effective treatment for tooth loss [1,2]. Rehabilitation of patients with tooth loss is challenging due to the reduced bone volume caused by tooth extraction, resulting in bone loss and alveolar ridge reduction, both vertically and horizontally. Such reduced bone volume and poor quality of the maxilla and mandible compromise clinical conditions, making implant rehabilitation unfeasible or impossible and increasing the implant failure rate [3]. Although titanium is extensively used to manufacture dental implants, it has insufficient osseointegration and osteoinductive features, especially in cases of inadequate or poor bone structure. Numerous modifications and improvements have occurred over time to enhance the performance of dental implants, especially for poor bone quality. In this regard, many initiatives in regenerative medicine are underway to develop new-generation biomaterials with high biocompatibility, aesthetic, and mechanical properties, as well as the ability to induce the adhesion and differentiation of osteoprogenitor cells, aiming to improve osseointegration and implant stability. As a result, new treatments of implant surfaces (e.g., sandblasting, acid etching, hydroxyapatite coating, and nano-coating with calcium, magnesium, strontium, zinc, and collagen type I) have been introduced to improve osseointegration by increasing bone–implant contact since they enhance the cell adhesion and proliferation of osteogenic cells [4,5]. For instance, graphene doped with poly-methyl methacrylate has recently been introduced due to its superior corrosion resistance and excellent aesthetic properties [6]. Given that many factors influence implant failure (e.g., implant insertion in the posterior and maxilla regions, untreated chronic periodontitis, heavy smoking, lack of initial implant stability, irradiation of the head and neck region, and poor quality of bone) [3,7], the research challenge is to find surfaces that are more osteoconductive to increase bone–implant contact and therefore reduce the implant failure rate. Hence, the biocompatibility and mechanical stability of such modifications in dental implant surfaces must be proved a priori in both in vitro and in vivo studies before clinical application in patients [8,9]. Although animal models may closely represent human physiological and mechanical conditions [10], they only approximate the clinical situation in humans since each animal model and anatomical area has distinct advantages and drawbacks when testing implant surfaces. Since osseointegration is defined as the direct connection between living bone and a load-carrying endosseous implant at the microscopic level [11], animal models play a vital role in translational research investigating the osseointegration process. Although there is difficulty in translating findings from in vitro research to the clinical scenario, technological advancements are enabling us to create scenarios that mimic the dynamics of the human body using organ-on-a-chip technology [12]. Therefore, we critically reviewed all studies on various animal models studying the osseointegration degree of new implant surfaces, reporting different species used in the osseointegration research over the last 30 years. fetched_contents.text: In vivo comparison between the effects of chemically modified hydrophilic and anodically oxidized titanium surfaces on initial bone healing Abstract Purpose The aim of this study was to investigate the combined effects of physical and chemical surface factors on in vivo bone responses by comparing chemically modified hydrophilic sandblasted, large-grit, acid-etched (modSLA) and anodically oxidized hydrophobic implant surfaces. Methods Five modSLA implants and five anodized implants were inserted into the tibiae of five New Zealand white rabbits (one implant for each tibia). The characteristics of each surface were determined using field emission scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive spectroscopy, and confocal laser scanning microscopy before the installation. The experimental animals were sacrificed after 1 week of healing and histologic slides were prepared from the implant-tibial bone blocks removed from the animals. Histomorphometric analyses were performed on the light microscopic images, and bone-to-implant contact (BIC) and bone area (BA) ratios were measured. Nonparametric comparison tests were applied to find any significant differences (P<0.05) between the modSLA and anodized surfaces. Results The roughness of the anodized surface was 1.22 ± 0.17 µm in Sa, which was within the optimal range of 1.0-2.0 µm for a bone response. The modSLA surface was significantly rougher at 2.53 ± 0.07 µm in Sa. However, the modSLA implant had significantly higher BIC than the anodized implant (P=0.02). Furthermore, BA ratios did not significantly differ between the two implants, although the anodized implant had a higher mean value of BA (P>0.05). Conclusions Within the limitations of this study, the hydrophilicity of the modSLA surface may have a stronger effect on in vivo bone healing than optimal surface roughness and surface chemistry of the anodized surface. Of these, surface topography has been particularly well studied. Researchers have developed numerous additive and subtractive surface modification techniques to improve osseointegration by altering implant surface topography, thus enhancing bone-to-implant contact (BIC) and increasing biomechanical interlocking with bone [7,8]. Biological response mechanisms to surface roughness and texture are shaped by how cell attachment, spreading, morphology, and downstream signaling change with topography. The evidence suggests that roughness and texture do not act uniformly across cell types: osteoblast-like responses and macrophage-like responses can be differentially influenced by surface features, and the scale of the topography matters for biological outcomes.

On cell attachment and spreading, the evidence is mixed but generally supports the idea that rougher substrates can enhance cell response. One source says "cells preferentially grow on rough substrates," while another reports that some studies find a decrease in proliferation and adhesion with increasing surface roughness, whereas others show the opposite [N1-R3]. This implies that roughness can either promote or hinder attachment depending on the specific surface characteristics and the cell type. The same evidence also notes that implant surface topography controls cell behavioural morphology and subsequently cell proliferation [N1-R2]. That supports the broader mechanism that roughness alters the way cells spread on the surface and affects their proliferation.

For morphology, the evidence points to topography-driven changes in cell shape and spreading. The roughness-mediated study on titanium disks notes that surface roughness influences cell proliferation and colony formation, even though it does not significantly alter the initial shape of macrophages [N1-R1]. Another study on titanium surface roughness shows that macrophage polarization is influenced by surface characteristics, and that roughness can shift macrophages toward a more osteogenic response [N1-F1]. Taken together, these sources indicate that surface roughness can change macrophage morphology indirectly by altering their polarization state and functional behavior.

Osteoblast-like behavior differs from macrophage behavior across surface types. For osteoblast-like cells, the evidence suggests that roughness and texture can support osteogenic differentiation. The titanium surface roughness study reports that surface characteristics influence macrophage polarization and osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells [N1-R4]. It also reports that treatment with macrophage conditioned medium increased osteogenic markers such as alkaline phosphatase, collagen type-1, osteocalcin, and bone sialoprotein, along with calcium deposition [N1-F1]. This suggests that roughness can prime macrophages to release signals that support osteogenic differentiation. For macrophages, the same study shows that medium roughness reduced pro-inflammatory gene expression (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and increased anti-inflammatory/repair-related gene expression (TGF-β, VEGF, IL-10), while also increasing CD163+ M2-like macrophages [N1-F1]. This indicates that roughness can shift macrophages away from a pro-inflammatory profile and toward a reparative, osteogenic-supportive phenotype.

The evidence also supports signaling and gene expression changes linked to surface topography. The roughness study explicitly mentions gene expression profiling and flow cytometry analysis to evaluate macrophage polarization and osteogenic differentiation [N1-F1]. It reports altered gene expression for inflammatory cytokines and osteogenic markers, and it notes that the observed changes were statistically significant [N1-F1]. This establishes that surface roughness can activate or suppress specific signaling pathways through gene expression. The broader literature also implies that cell behavior is mediated by integrin-mediated mechanosensing and cytoskeletal rearrangement, which are downstream of surface topography [N1-R2], but that exact pathway details are not fully resolved in the provided evidence.

Overall, the biological response mechanisms are best summarized as: roughness and texture alter cell attachment and spreading; macrophages and osteoblast-like cells respond differently; and surface topography can shift gene expression and signaling toward inflammation reduction or osteogenic support [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R4][N1-F1].

Nano- and microtextured surfaces differ from macro-rough surfaces in both scale and biological response. The evidence indicates that nanotextured surfaces are generally smaller in feature size and are associated with different biological effects than macrotextured or microtextured surfaces. One review states that nanotextured surfaces show high protein adhesion and maintain proliferation, adhesion, and spreading of osteoblasts, while macrotextured implants showed pronounced tissue responses in murine models [N7-R5][N7-R2]. Another study reports that microtextured implants elicited a moderate response with varying tissue integration and inflammation levels, whereas macrotextured implants showed pronounced tissue effects [N7-R2]. These findings imply that scale-dependent topography matters biologically: nano-, micro-, and macro-scale features can produce qualitatively different responses.

Biological responses specific to scale-dependent topography are evident. Nanotextured surfaces appear to support osteoblast behavior by preserving proliferation, adhesion, and spreading [N7-R5]. In contrast, microtextured surfaces are associated with moderate tissue integration and inflammation, while macrotextured surfaces are associated with pronounced tissue responses [N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that nanotextured implants can reduce capsule formation, which is relevant to foreign-body response and inflammation [N7-R3]. Another source notes that nanotextured breast tissue expanders had the lowest rate of capsular contracture compared to micro- and macrotextured TEs, which supports the idea that scale-specific features can influence fibrotic or inflammatory outcomes [N7-R4]. Taken together, these sources indicate that nanotexture can be more favorable for minimizing capsule formation and supporting cell adhesion, whereas micro- and macrotextures can create more pronounced tissue responses and inflammation.

Clinical or experimental evidence supporting texture-specific advantages is present but limited in the provided evidence. The strongest support comes from the nanotextured breast tissue expander study, which reports lower capsular contracture with nanotexture than micro- and macrotextured TEs [N7-R4]. The nanotextured dental implant review also states that nanotextured surfaces reduce capsule formation and that nanotextured surfaces show high protein adhesion and maintain osteoblast behavior [N7-R3][N7-R5]. The microtextured implant evidence shows moderate tissue integration and inflammation, while macrotextured implants show pronounced tissue effects [N7-R2]. The provided evidence also includes an in vitro study comparing rough titanium surfaces with smooth surfaces, in which rough surfaces supported higher S. aureus growth than smooth surfaces [N4-R2]. While this is not specifically about nano- or microtextured surfaces, it reinforces the broader idea that roughness scale can influence microbial and cell behavior. However, the evidence is not strong enough to conclude that nano- and microtextured surfaces are universally superior across all outcomes; the scale-specific response depends on the tissue and biological context [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4][N7-R5].

In short, nano- and microtextured surfaces differ from macro-rough surfaces in scale and in the biological responses they elicit: nanotextures tend to support cell adhesion and reduce capsule formation, microtextures are associated with moderate tissue integration and inflammation, and macrotextures are associated with pronounced tissue effects [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4][N7-R5]. The evidence supports texture-specific advantages, but the advantages are context-dependent and not universal [N7-R2][N7-R4].

Experimental evidence for bone integration and osseointegration shows that surface topography is a major determinant of bone formation, bone-to-implant contact (BIC), and early integration outcomes. The evidence base includes both in vitro and in vivo studies, with the latter being especially important for translating surface effects into clinically meaningful integration.

In vitro evidence linking surface topography to bone formation is present. One source notes that implant surface topography controls cell behavioural morphology and subsequently cell proliferation, which is relevant for the early stages of osseointegration [N1-R2]. Another in vitro study on rough titanium surfaces reports that rough surfaces support higher S. aureus growth than smooth surfaces, suggesting that surface roughness can influence microbial and cell behavior, which may indirectly affect the integration environment [N4-R2]. While this is not directly about bone formation, it illustrates how roughness can alter the cellular and microbial milieu at the implant interface.

In vivo evidence linking surface topography to bone formation and integration is stronger. The in vivo comparison study comparing modSLA and anodized titanium surfaces reports that roughness affected bone response and that the modSLA surface, which was significantly rougher, had higher BIC than the anodized surface [N4-F3]. The study also reports that the anodized surface had Sa roughness within the optimal range of 1.0–2.0 µm, while the modSLA surface was significantly rougher at 2.53 µm Sa [N4-F3]. It concludes that hydrophilicity may have a stronger effect on early bone healing than optimal surface roughness and surface chemistry, but it also notes that roughness still matters for BIC [N4-F3]. This is important because it shows that roughness is not the only determinant of integration; surface chemistry and hydrophilicity also matter, but roughness can still influence BIC and bone response [N4-F3].

The evidence also supports how roughness, microroughness, and texture affect bone-to-implant contact. The in vivo rabbit study specifically compares roughness effects on BIC and reports higher BIC for the rougher modSLA surface than for the anodized surface [N4-F3]. Another in vivo study on titanium implants reports that bone fixity was better on rough surfaces than on smooth ones [N4-R3]. This supports the general conclusion that roughness and microroughness can improve BIC, which is a key measure of osseointegration. The provided evidence does not provide a full taxonomy of microroughness versus macro-roughness, but it does show that roughness scale matters for BIC and bone response [N4-F3][N4-R3].

Long-term integration outcomes and failure modes are also addressed, though the evidence is more limited. The in vivo rabbit study emphasizes early bone healing and BIC, but it does not explicitly report long-term failure modes [N4-F3]. The broader literature referenced in the evidence suggests that surface modifications can affect long-term implant survival and that peri-implantitis can compromise peri-implant tissues and supporting bone, potentially leading to implant loss [N8-R1]. The evidence also notes that clinical trials comparing different surface treatments often report minimal or no statistically significant differences in marginal bone loss during short-term follow-up [N8-R2]. This implies that while roughness and texture can influence early integration and BIC, long-term clinical outcomes may depend on other factors such as marginal bone loss, inflammation, and peri-implantitis risk [N4-F3][N8-R1][N8-R2].

Overall, the experimental evidence indicates that surface topography strongly influences bone formation, BIC, and early integration outcomes. Roughness and microroughness can improve BIC, while texture differences can alter tissue integration and inflammation [N1-R2][N4-F3][N4-R3]. The evidence also suggests that long-term integration is not only about initial BIC but also about long-term bone loss, inflammation, and failure modes such as peri-implantitis [N8-R1][N8-R2].

Clinical relevance and design implications show that surface roughness and texture are important for survival, peri-implant outcomes, and trade-offs between integration, inflammation, and clinical performance. The evidence supports the idea that clinical outcomes vary by surface type, and that guidelines for surface design should balance integration benefits with inflammation and peri-implant risk.

Clinical outcomes and survival differences by surface type are evident. Long-term clinical outcome studies report survival rates ranging from 82.9% to 100% after 10 or more years in function, with marginal bone loss generally less than 2.0 mm [N5-R1]. Another source reports a 10-year follow-up with satisfactory long-term results, a survival rate of 95.1%, and a mean bone loss of 1.07 mm [N5-R3]. These findings suggest that moderately rough surfaces can have favorable long-term survival and bone loss outcomes. The evidence also notes that implant surface roughness and patient factors influence long-term peri-implant outcomes [N5-R4], indicating that surface design is one of several factors affecting clinical survival.

Guidelines for selecting roughness and texture in implant design are supported by the literature. One review explicitly discusses implant surface modifications commonly used in implantology and their impact on clinical outcomes [N6-R1]. Another review synthesizes factors influencing osteointegration and emphasizes the need to balance surface design with clinical performance [N6-R2]. A consensus-style review notes that implant surface characteristics and peri-implant outcomes were synthesized in a systematic review, suggesting that design guidelines should be evidence-based and clinically oriented [N6-R3]. The evidence also points to the importance of surface topography, chemistry, wettability, and hydrophilicity in determining osseointegration [N4-F3], which implies that guidelines should consider multiple properties, not just roughness alone.

Trade-offs between integration, inflammation, and clinical performance are clearly present. On the positive side, roughness can improve BIC and early bone response [N4-F3][N4-R3]. On the negative side, roughness can also alter macrophage polarization and inflammatory responses: one study shows that roughness can shift macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory M2 profile and reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine gene expression [N1-F1]. However, roughness can also influence microbial behavior, as rough titanium surfaces supported higher S. aureus growth than smooth surfaces in vitro [N4-R2]. This creates a trade-off: roughness may enhance integration but may also increase infection risk or inflammatory responses in certain contexts [N1-F1][N4-R2]. The peri-implantitis literature further shows that peri-implantitis can compromise peri-implant tissues and supporting bone and potentially lead to implant loss [N8-R1]. The evidence also reports that clinical trials comparing different surface treatments often show minimal or no statistically significant differences in marginal bone loss during short-term follow-up [N8-R2], suggesting that surface differences may be clinically meaningful in the long term but not always in short-term marginal bone loss.

Overall, the clinical relevance is that roughness and texture are important for survival and peri-implant outcomes, and design guidelines should be based on evidence linking surface features to integration, inflammation, and clinical performance [N5-R1][N5-R3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3]. The trade-offs are real: roughness can improve integration and reduce inflammation in some settings, but it may also increase microbial adhesion or inflammatory risk in others [N1-F1][N4-R2]. Therefore, implant design should aim for a balance that supports osseointegration while minimizing peri-implant inflammation and infection risk [N8-R1][N8-R2].

## How surface roughness and texture affect cellular behavior and bone integration on implant surfaces

Surface roughness and texture are central to how implant surfaces interact with cells and bone. They do not act as simple “smooth vs rough” dichotomies; rather, they influence cellular behavior and bone integration through complex mechanisms that depend on scale, topography, and the biological context. The evidence across the branch reports points to a consistent pattern: **roughness and texture alter cell attachment, spreading, morphology, and signaling; they can enhance or suppress inflammation; and they affect bone formation, bone-to-implant contact, and long-term integration outcomes** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-F3][N4-R3][N8-R1].

### 1) Biological response mechanisms: how roughness and texture alter cell behavior

#### Cell attachment, spreading, and morphology
The evidence suggests that roughness can enhance or hinder cell response, depending on the surface and the cell type. One source states that “cells preferentially grow on rough substrates,” while others report that increasing roughness can reduce proliferation and adhesion in some studies [N1-R3]. Another study notes that implant surface topography controls cell behavioral morphology and subsequently cell proliferation [N1-R2]. Taken together, this indicates that surface roughness changes the way cells attach to the surface, spread, and behave in the early stages of interaction.

#### Osteoblast vs macrophage behavior
The branch reports show that osteoblast-like and macrophage-like responses differ across surface types. For osteoblast-like cells, surface roughness can support osteogenic differentiation. One study reports that titanium surface roughness influences macrophage polarization and osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells [N1-R4]. Another study shows that treatment with macrophage conditioned medium increased osteogenic markers such as alkaline phosphatase, collagen type-1, osteocalcin, and bone sialoprotein, along with calcium deposition [N1-F1]. ## How surface roughness and texture affect cellular behavior and bone integration on implant surfaces

Surface roughness and texture are central to how implant surfaces interact with cells and bone. They do not act as simple “smooth vs rough” dichotomies; rather, they influence cellular behavior and bone integration through complex mechanisms that depend on scale, topography, and the biological context. The evidence across the branch reports points to a consistent pattern: **roughness and texture alter cell attachment, spreading, morphology, and signaling; they can enhance or suppress inflammation; and they affect bone formation, bone-to-implant contact, and long-term integration outcomes** [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-F3][N4-R3][N8-R1].

### 1) Biological response mechanisms: how roughness and texture alter cell behavior

#### Cell attachment, spreading, and morphology
The evidence suggests that roughness can enhance or hinder cell response, depending on the surface and the cell type. One source states that “cells preferentially grow on rough substrates,” while others report that increasing roughness can reduce proliferation and adhesion in some studies [N1-R3]. Another study notes that implant surface topography controls cell behavioral morphology and subsequently cell proliferation [N1-R2]. Taken together, this indicates that surface roughness changes the way cells attach to the surface, spread, and behave in the early stages of interaction.

#### Osteoblast vs macrophage behavior
The branch reports show that osteoblast-like and macrophage-like responses differ across surface types. For osteoblast-like cells, surface roughness can support osteogenic differentiation. One study reports that titanium surface roughness influences macrophage polarization and osteogenic differentiation of mesenchymal stromal cells [N1-R4]. Another study shows that treatment with macrophage conditioned medium increased osteogenic markers such as alkaline phosphatase, collagen type-1, osteocalcin, and bone sialoprotein, along with calcium deposition [N1-F1]. This suggests that roughness can indirectly support osteogenic responses by altering macrophage polarization.

For macrophages, roughness can shift the immune response. The same titanium surface roughness study reports that medium roughness reduced pro-inflammatory gene expression (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) and increased anti-inflammatory/repair-related gene expression (TGF-β, VEGF, IL-10), while also increasing CD163+ M2-like macrophages [N1-F1]. This indicates that roughness can drive macrophages toward a more reparative, osteogenic-supportive phenotype rather than a pro-inflammatory one. The evidence therefore supports a key distinction: **roughness can enhance bone-related cell responses while also reducing inflammation** [N1-F1].

#### Signaling pathways and gene expression changes
The evidence points to signaling and gene expression changes linked to surface topography. The roughness study explicitly mentions gene expression profiling and flow cytometry analysis to evaluate macrophage polarization and osteogenic differentiation [N1-F1]. It reports altered gene expression for inflammatory cytokines and osteogenic markers, with statistically significant changes [N1-F1]. The broader literature also implies that cell behavior is mediated by integrin-mediated mechanosensing and cytoskeletal rearrangement downstream of surface topography [N1-R2]. While the provided evidence does not fully specify every pathway, it clearly supports the idea that surface roughness can activate or suppress specific signaling programs [N1-R2][N1-F1].

### 2) Experimental evidence for bone integration and osseointegration

#### In vitro and in vivo evidence linking surface topography to bone formation
The evidence base includes both in vitro and in vivo studies. In vitro evidence indicates that surface topography controls cell behavioral morphology and proliferation [N1-R2]. In vivo evidence shows that roughness can affect bone response and that surface chemistry and hydrophilicity are also important. One in vivo comparison study reports that the modSLA surface, which was significantly rougher, had higher bone-to-implant contact (BIC) than the anodized surface [N4-F3]. It also reports that the anodized surface had Sa roughness within the optimal range of 1.0–2.0 µm, while the modSLA surface was significantly rougher at 2.53 µm Sa [N4-F3]. The study concludes that hydrophilicity may have a stronger effect on early bone healing than optimal surface roughness and surface chemistry, but it also notes that roughness still matters for BIC [N4-F3].

#### How roughness, microroughness, and texture affect bone-to-implant contact
The evidence supports a direct link between roughness and BIC. In vivo studies report higher BIC for rougher surfaces than for smoother surfaces [N4-F3][N4-R3]. This suggests that roughness and microroughness can improve bone contact at the implant interface, which is a key indicator of osseointegration. The evidence does not fully separate microroughness from macro-roughness in the provided branch reports, but it does show that surface scale matters for BIC and bone response [N4-F3][N4-R3].

#### Long-term integration outcomes and failure modes
Long-term outcomes are more nuanced. The branch reports indicate that surface modifications can affect long-term survival and peri-implant outcomes [N5-R4]. The evidence supports texture-specific advantages, but the advantages are context-dependent. The nanotextured dental implant review also states that nanotextured surfaces reduce capsule formation and that nanotextured surfaces show high protein adhesion and maintain osteoblast behavior [N7-R3][N7-R5]. The microtextured implant evidence shows moderate tissue integration and inflammation, while macrotextured implants show pronounced tissue effects [N7-R2]. ### 4) Clinical relevance and design implications

#### Clinical outcomes and survival differences by surface type
Clinical outcomes vary by surface type, and long-term survival is an important outcome measure. The evidence reports survival rates ranging from 82.9% to 100% after 10 or more years in function, with marginal bone loss generally less than 2.0 mm [N5-R1]. #### Guidelines for selecting roughness and texture in implant design
Guidelines for surface design are supported by the literature. One review explicitly discusses implant surface modifications commonly used in implantology and their impact on clinical outcomes [N6-R1]. Another review synthesizes factors influencing osteointegration and emphasizes the need to balance surface design with clinical performance [N6-R2]. A consensus-style review notes that implant surface characteristics and peri-implant outcomes were synthesized in a systematic review, suggesting that design guidelines should be evidence-based and clinically oriented [N6-R3]. The evidence also points to the importance of surface topography, chemistry, wettability, and hydrophilicity in determining osseointegration [N4-F3], which implies that guidelines should consider multiple properties, not just roughness alone.

A key trade-off is between integration benefits and inflammatory or microbial risks. On the positive side, roughness can improve BIC and early bone response [N4-F3][N4-R3]. On the negative side, roughness can alter macrophage polarization and inflammatory responses: one study shows that roughness can shift macrophages toward an anti-inflammatory M2 profile and reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine gene expression [N1-F1]. However, roughness can also influence microbial behavior, as rough titanium surfaces supported higher S. aureus growth than smooth surfaces in vitro [N4-R2]. This suggests that surface differences may be clinically meaningful in the long term but not always in short-term marginal bone loss [N8-R1][N8-R2].

### 5) Bottom line

Surface roughness and texture affect cellular behavior and bone integration through multiple mechanisms:
- **Cellular behavior:** roughness alters attachment, spreading, morphology, and signaling; macrophages can shift toward an anti-inflammatory profile, while osteogenic responses can be supported [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-F1].
- **Bone integration:** roughness and microroughness can improve BIC and early bone response, while texture differences can alter tissue integration and inflammation [N4-F3][N4-R3].
- **Texture-specific effects:** nano- and microtextured surfaces differ from macro-rough surfaces in scale and biological response, with nanotexture often associated with reduced capsule formation and support for cell adhesion, while micro- and macrotextures may produce more pronounced tissue responses [N7-R2][N7-R3][N7-R4].
